section: 1.6.4.8. Tempo-spatial influence race diversity: The change in pathogen
text: The avr genes of the pathogen interacts with R genes of the host to induce the host defenses that prevent host infection and limit pathogen multiplication in a suicidal manner in host tissues. In rice, lesion length or type is often used as indicator of R gene function after infection by a pathogen. The avr genes may shorten the lesion length or change the lesion types from acute to necrotic. By mid-1990s, more than 40 avr genes were identified among pathogenic Xanthomonas spp. and all belonged to the avrBs3/pthA or avr/pth gene family (Leach and White 1996). In the rice-Xoo system, most of the avr genes were identified through specific race-rice genotype interactions and from strains of PXO86, PXO99, and JXOIII. The avr genes cloned from Xoo isolates were avrXa10, avrXa7, avrxa5, avrXa3, and avrXa27. The main function of avr genes is to direct recognition, which can lead to race-specific resistance based on the gene-for-gene interactions. However, it was found later that some members of the avr gene family contribute to pathogenic aggressiveness (Ponciano et al 2003). The proteins secreted by the pathogens into the host cells are termed as "effectors" and these have two different functions, an elicitor function that induces resistance, and a virulence function that suppresses expression of resistance (van Dijk et al 1999). Some effectors appear to play double roles, causing host cell-death in incompatible interactions (resistant variety) or suppressing host resistance for disease development in compatible interactions (susceptible varieties) (Alfano and Collmer 2004). The recognition between host and bacterial pathogen occurs inside the host plant cells (Gopalan et al 1996; Vivian and Arnold 2000).

section: 1.5.1.3. Disease development in problem soils. BSp is known to be a disease closely
text: associated with poor soils that are deficient in nutrients or in which toxic substance have accumulated, stressing the rice plants and thus predisposing them to infection (Baba 1957, Goto 1958, Sato 1964-65). Ou (1985) provided a more comprehensive review on the effects of problem soils on the occurrence of BSp, summarized as follows. In Japan, BSp often occurs in a soil condition known as "akiochi", in which the soil is deficient in silica, potassium, manganese, or magnesium and where hydrogen sulfide has evolved causing foot rot. Under such conditions, the rice plant is attacked more easily by B. oryzae, especially when nitrogen is deficient at the late tillering stage. However, nitrogen deficiency can be reversed when adequate nitrogen is applied. It should be noted that BSp can occur in soils that are deficient or excessive in nitrogen (Chattopadhyay and Dickson 1960). However, information on occurrence of BSp in soil excessive in nitrogen may not be as conclusive as it is in deficient soils. In contrast to other essential elements, more phosphorus in the soil may actually induce more BSp on rice plants. Excessive hydrogen sulfide in the soil inhibits rice's absorption of nutrients and water and causes an imbalance in nutrient uptake. Soil high in organic matter content, such as butyric and acetic acids, may also produce the same effect as nutrient deficiency on BSp development.

In addition to the pathogens described in the previous chapters, several other groups of pathogens or opportunistic pathogens attack rice grains. They can be grouped under the "grain discoloration or dirty panicle" syndrome. Individually, they do not cause alarming damage to rice and there are no distinct and characteristic symptoms caused by individual agents. However, they proliferate under favorable circumstances created when panicles are exposed to a sudden rainstorm or heavy rainfall. When crop lodging occurs at the mature stage prior to harvest, panicles come in contact with the ground. The fungi usually detected on rice seeds consist mostly of these pathogens. Those listed here are described in Ou (1985) and also appear in many Japanese literature citations on grain diseases.

The best option in managing grain discoloration is to encourage farmers to use clean seed for planting. In the past, seed health has been considered only in the context of plant quarantine regulations. The importance of some seedborne pathogens cannot and should not be ignored for plant quarantine purposes, germplasm exchange, and seed trading. Several seedborne pathogens have quarantine importance in seed movement and in exchange or rice trading. The pathogen infects seed, which is the most important vehicle for movement and dissemination of pathogens, such as Tilletia horrida (causal organism of kernel smut) and Aphelenchoides besseyi (causal nematode of white-tip). Both diseases can be properly managed and minimized in the field by using healthy or clean seed for planting.

section: 12.6.6.  Effect of silica on blast development. Besides climatic factors, blast
text: development is also influenced by nutritional factors. Among these, silica is of particular interest because of its wide and affordable availability to rice farmers and noticeable effect on suppression of blast development. Its effect and function have been investigated by many scientists since the early years but new insights of its mechanism have been revealed only recently. Silicate compounds have been intensively promoted for soil amendment to blast control since a silicate slag from a blast furnace can provide a practical and affordable silica source for rice fertilizer (Ohta et al 1953, Snyder et al 1986). Silica application has effectively reduced blast incidence (Datnoff et al 1991, Ishiguro 2001), but its efficacy is related to the particle size (RBl Table 4; Datnoff et al 1992). Many scientists have already studied the effects of silica on blast development even in the earlier years (Ou 1985). The findings, as summarized by Ou (1985), showed that rice plants with a high silica content seemed to show less damage on silicated epidermal cells and decreased infection. Some believed that the silicated epidermal cells could have prevented physical penetration of the fungus (Hemmi 1933). Others indicated that the effect of a physical barrier subscribed to only part of the resistance induced by silica and it might be more related to lowering nitrogen absorption (Ishibashi 1936, Akimoto 1939, Ishizuka and Hayakawa 1951). Thus, the degree of resistance was correlated not only with silica content but also with the decrease in nitrogen content. RBl Table 4. In systems where water supply is not assured, or "rainfed rice" systems, the crop depends entirely on rainfall for water. On relatively flat, often lowland, topography, or where fields have been leveled, farmers normally construct bunds to capture and hold rainwater. In years with abundant well-distributed rainfall, rainfed lowlands may approach irrigated yield potential. Standing water rarely, if ever, accumulates in the fields and yields are typically very low. The risk of crop failure is so high under both rainfed lowland and upland conditions that farmers are often unwilling to invest much in fertilizer applications. Yields therefore tend to be low, and as will be seen in some chapters, disease pressure also tends to be lower. Rainfed upland systems were more common in the past and increasingly are now found only in areas with limited market access or where lands are being opened for other ultimate purposes. Most rice in the world-that is, in Asia-is transplanted. Typically, seedlings are grown in high density in a "nursery" until they are anywhere from 15 to 30 days, or more, old.

The first spread of BB and its corresponding damage in Japan are worth mentioning. Prior to cultivation of modern varieties, occasional BB damage was reported but there were no real data on yield loss. As early as 1908-10, BB occurred in almost all the southwestern parts of Japan, which gradually spread to the northern parts in the 1960s. section: 4.2. Epidemics: their relation to yield losses and the gain potential from
text: Production situations and crop health syndromes are not site-specific; to the contrary, most are shared by sites that can be geographically very far apart. • A strong association between production situations and crop health syndromes has been demonstrated (Savary et al 2011). Bayesian methods have been used to predict crop health syndromes from production situations; • There are strong interactions among diseases in their yield-reducing effects. Overall, these interactions lead to a less-than-additive effect of accumulated injuries on the resulting yield losses. • Two approaches, simulation modeling and multivariate statistical prediction, yielded similar outcomes on the yield-reducing effect of diseases, alone or combined, in a range of characterized production situations, on yield losses. The above summary addresses only direct, quantitative, and biomass losses. It may very well be that major efforts, similar to those deployed in the USA and Europe to address fusarium head blight in wheat (Paul et al 2010), might be required to control emerging, quality-affecting rice diseases, such as brown spot and false smut.

GlB was first found in the USA and Japan but it is now widely reported in many rice-growing countries in Asia, the Americas, and Africa (Ou 1985). It is a minor disease. If infection occurs early and under favorable conditions, grains may not form. Late infection may result in partly filled grains or discolored and brittle grains. Thus, like other grain diseases except false smut, in combination with other grain infections, GlB may cause some losses in rice yield.

section: Section 2. Bacterial diseases / Chapter  3. Leaf sheath diseases / Introduction
text: Sheath browning and grain discoloration can be caused by both fungi and pathogenic bacteria (Ou 1985; Cottyn et al 1996a,b). Sheath browning is a common syndrome on rice crops grown during rainy season in tropical environments. Various degrees of browning, from light brown to dark brown, may be observed on the leaf sheath at the booting stage. Some of the leaf sheath browning may be similar to that of bacterial sheath brown rot while others to sheath rot. Similar situations are also observed in grain discoloration. Isolation from infected tissues of the causative pathogen yields different, and often more than one, bacteria mentioned in this chapter, yet the symptoms are not distinguishable from those caused by an individual bacterium reported in the literature. One may assume that the distribution of these bacteria is commonly associated with the cultivation of the semidwarf modern rice varieties in the rainy season. Rice plants under stress are predisposed to invasion by pathogenic bacteria. Although there are reports of an antagonistic effect of some of the bacterial pathogens isolated from seed or the leaf sheath, there is little information on interaction among these bacteria in actual disease development in situ synergistically or antagonistically. However, research in disease development and design of disease management requires considering all pathogens together rather than as an individual bacterium. Pseudomonas fuscovaginae, P. syringae pv. syringae, B. glumae, A. avenae subsp. avenae, and many others that infect the flag leaf sheath and rice grain are distributed worldwide. P. fuscovaginae, which supposedly causes sheath brown rot at lower temperatures, is also often isolated together with P. syringae pv. syringae and other bacteria from leaf sheath showing sheath rot and discolored grains.

section: 1.4.1. Primary inocula. The teliospores are the resting spore structure for over­
text: It is mysterious in nature as how this is timed so accurately between the pathogen and the host to continue the infection process. There appears to be a "safety mechanism" to make sure that the teliospores germinate at the right time, i.e., when the host plant is at the most susceptible stage (Carris et al 2006). The actual penetration process of T. horrida into the host tissue is not known but is postulated as follows: "the sporidia land on the feathery stigma and penetrate through the style to the chalazas end of the ovary" (proposed by Sing and Pavgi 1973, as cited by Carris et al 2006). The fungus causes local infection of the florets by sporidia but not the leaves of the seedlings as postulated by Chowdhury (1946) and confirmed by Templeton (1961) who showed that the sporidia infected the opening flowers and later that the developing grains became smutted. There is no information on whether the teliospores of T. horrida can spread through air and can be carried by air currents for long-distance dispersal. However, it is known that kernel smut fungus can spread via infected seed, which is perhaps the most effective mechanism by which T. horrida has "traveled" around the world throughout most rice-growing regions. The teliospores are released from smutted grains before or during harvest, thus, contaminating healthy kernels, crop debris, and soil. Seedborne teliospores are the most important source of overwintering or off-season resting body, although there were reports of soilborne inoculum of teliospores (Biswas 2003). The survival of T. horrida as soilborne inoculum remains uncertain based on the available information.

The disease is usually found on the leaf sheath near the water line. Initially, it appears as a small, yellow, water-soaked spot, which gradually enlarges to 1-2 cm with an oblong shape or elliptical outline. The surface of the spot becomes reticulated from the presence of numerous dark brown lines that give it a net-like appearance. The area of infected parts of the sheaths often becomes whitish. Leaf blades of infected sheath turn yellow and eventually die. Infection of Cercospora janseana (narrow brown leaf spot) is frequently common on the sheath during the late stages of crop growth (unlike SnB of rice, which infects mainly the basal sheath) causing strikingly similar symptoms with dark brown cell walls and tan-to-yellow intercellular spaces giving a net-like pattern. It is also referred to simply as "net blotch" or as "sheath net blotch" in Texas and Louisiana U.S.A and can be mistaken as sheath net blotch caused by C. scoparium.

section: 4.3. Genus Oryzavirus: Rice ragged stunt virus (RRSV)
text: RRSV is another virus disease infecting rice that is transmitted by the brown planthopper in a persistent propagative manner and is the type species in the genus Oryzavirus in the Reoviridae family. RRSV is one of the economically important virus diseases in several Southeast and East Asia. RRSV outbreaks have been reported, especially in Indonesia, the Philippines, and Thailand during 1977-90. An RRSV outbreak in 2005 was reported in Vietnam (Cabauatan et al 2009) and found to be coinfecting with RGSV, resulting in a more severe yellowing syndrome causing significant yield loss (Du et al 2007). Another virus that was reported coinfecting RRSV is SRBSDV resulting in more aggravated disease symptoms. Wang et al (2014) conducted field investigations on insect interactions and found that WBPH and BPH transmitted SRBSDV and RRSV, respectively. They found that the virus-free WBPHs significantly preferred to feed on infected rice plants rather than on healthy plants and virus-free BPHs significantly preferred healthy plants. However, the RRSV-carrying BPHs preferred SRBSDV-infected rice plants. With these results, they have indicated that SRBSDV might assist RRSV transmission and infection.

In the Philippines, some earlier reports on RT-like diseases, except those of Fajardo et al (1964), emphasized their similarities to "rice dwarf" or "rice stunt" (Agati and Peralta 1939, Agati et al 1941, Reyes 1957, Serrano 1957) reported in Japan (Iida 1969, Iida and Shinakai 1969). Apparently, RT is different from rice dwarf or rice stripe in symptomatology and transmission manner (Iida 1969, Ling 1972). In surveys on "accep na pula" for several seasons from 1939 to 1941 in the Philippines, annual rice losses were estimated at 1.36 million tons, equivalent to 30% of total production (Serrano 1957). In a transmission test using Nn, three of seven leafhoppers subjected to three consecutive daily access feedings transmitted "tungro disease" in the first feeding, but not in later feedings. At IRRI, Laguna, Philippines, a similar disease was observed in 1963 and identified as a virus disease transmitted by GLH and called "tungro" (RT), although the virus agent was not known (Rivera and Ou 1965). In 1964, RT damaged rice on 10,000 hectares (Ou and Ling 1966). Major outbreaks of RT occurred in central Luzon damaging 100,000 hectares in 1970, 8,000 in 1971, and 40,000 in 1972 (Anjaneyulu et al 1994, Ling et al 1983, Reddy 1973). In another estimate, RT damaged 61,000 tons of rough rice valued at USD 2.2 million on about 70,000 hectares during the 1971 wet season alone (Reyes 1989). Total losses in the Philippines during 1969-72 were estimated at 5.3 million tons (Reddy 1973).

section: 6.5.3. Pathogen specialization. Diverse cultural characteristics have been ob­
text: served on the fungus. Variations in conidial production were also noted among isolates when grown in liquid media (Singh and Gupta 1985). Based on the morphology of M. albescens in liquid culture media, Parkinson (1980) distinguished four main groups of the pathogen based on the abundance of aerial hyphae, conidial mass produced, and intensity of the mycelial pigmentation. However, in vitro fungal morphology should be treated cautiously when the information is used to relate to virulence (Turner and Black 2001). Turner and Black (2001) recognized distinctive patterns of host-pathogen interactions whenthey tested isolates from different geographical regions on a number of rice varieties (LSc Figure 5). Isolates 20.13 and 20.20 were virulent on rice variety ITA 306 while isolate 20.19 showed moderate virulence on this variety. Isolates 20.13 and 20.19 were virulent while isolate 20.20 seemed to be less virulent on variety SIPI. Although Turner and Black (2001) showed little information on host-pathogen interaction, the study did suggest possible physiologic specialization of the LSc fungus on different rice genotypes.

As the causal bacterium is seed-transmitted, Fang et al (1957) suggested imposing a quarantine regulation on rice seed movement from southern China. The causal bacteria had been detected on rice seed and seed transmission appears to be one of the most significant means for its long-distance dissemination. However, there is no actual data available to indicate that the occurrence of BLS at 28-30°C. in other countries or districts was a result of Source: C.M. Vera Cruz, pers. comm. seed introduction. Whether or not infected straw or rice plant debris provided inocula for BLS development was uncertain (Shekhawat and Srivastava 1972b). However, seed transmission may be of less significance for off-season (winter) crops sown with seed produced in the main season (summer) because the disease does not develop in cool, dry conditions (Rao 1987). The bacterial cells ooze out of the infected tissues in humid conditions during rice crop growth. The ooze on the lesion surface may dry up to become very small amber-colored beads. When these beads are moistened by dew or rain, the bacterial cells in these beads are dispersed and spread through wind-blown rain water and leaf contact to cause new infections on the same leaf or on other leaves thus serving as inoculum for secondary infection.

section: 1.5.2.3. Detection using molecular tools: Amplification of primer-specific DNA
text: Of the 10 tested seeds collected in Pila, five were positive for both expected PCR bands, three were positive for 497-bp band only, and two did not produce any amplification product. None of the 10 seeds from samples collected in Quezon showed any PCR product. To compare the efficiency of the PCR assay versus the method of dilution plating on XOS medium, seed washes from 10-g batches of naturally and artificially Xoocontaminated seeds were diluted and then plated on XOS medium. Colonies of Xoo strain PXO340 were recovered on XOS medium from seed wash of IRBB10 seeds soaked in bacterial suspension at 3x108 CFU/ml, but not from 2x105 CFU/ml (BB Table 4). Several attempts to recover Xoo on XOS medium after germination of artificially contaminated IRBB10 seeds were not successful. Xoo was not detected on XOS medium by dilution plating of seed washes from seed samples harvested from diseased rice plants in farmer's fields. section: 1.5.1.4. Disease development in relation to climatic factors. Padmanabhan (1973)
text: The results of these efforts are remarkable that these three diseases are no longer a major threat (except endemic in some countries where resistance breeding and research in relation to resistance breeding have been ignored). This is a positive consequence of a well-focused effort targeting varietal improvement on a few major production constraints. The negative aspect, however, especially from a disease research point-of-view, is the total neglect of research being done on a few other potential threatening diseases, including BSp. The fact that the disease usually occurs on plants growing under stress induced by poor soil conditions and moisture regimes poses some problems. These include being able to artificially infect plants with the BSp pathogen on either a limited number of experimental plants or artificially creating an epidemic situation in a disease nursery designed for large-scale evaluation of germplasm. This has deterred investigations on this disease compared with well researched diseases. However, some research on BSp is reappearing. Whether it will continue or not remains to be seen. Despite the fact that BSp has been associated with one of the worst rice disease epidemics in history, research on this disease, including epidemiology, remains meager.
